transcript.heading: News Report One (British Male)
paras: A new study has found that drinking coffee in moderation may be linked to a lower risk of several chronic diseases and a longer lifespan, according to researchers at the University of Oxford. The study analyzed data from over 500,000 people and found that those who drank two to three cups of coffee per day had a lower risk of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, and certain types of cancer compared to those who didn't drink coffee. They also had a slightly lower risk of death from all causes during the study period. Both regular and decaffeinated coffee showed similar benefits, suggesting that caffeine isn't the only factor—coffee contains hundreds of different compounds, including antioxidants and anti-inflammatory substances, that may contribute to its health effects. However, researchers caution that more research is needed, and that very high coffee consumption (more than six cups a day) may have negative effects. They also note that adding lots of sugar, cream, or syrups to coffee can cancel out many of its health benefits.
Questions 1 and 2 are based on the news report you have just heard.
1. What did the University of Oxford study find about coffee?
2. Why might coffee have health benefits according to researchers?

transcript.heading: News Report Two (American Female)
paras: The city of San Francisco has become the first major city in the United States to require all new buildings to have solar panels on their roofs, as part of the city's goal to run on 100 percent renewable energy by 2030. The rule applies to all new residential and commercial buildings under 10 stories tall, and it requires that solar panels cover at least 15 percent of the roof area. The city says the requirement will help reduce greenhouse gas emissions, create jobs in the solar industry, and save building owners money on their electricity bills over time. San Francisco already has some of the most ambitious climate goals in the country, and this new requirement is just one part of the city's plan to become carbon neutral. Critics argue that the requirement will increase the cost of new housing in a city where housing is already very expensive, but supporters say the long-term savings on electricity will more than make up for the initial cost.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Male)
paras: Archaeologists in Egypt have discovered the remains of a 2,000-year-old Roman temple in the city of Alexandria, according to a statement from the Egyptian Ministry of Antiquities. The temple, which dates back to the Roman period of Egyptian history, is believed to have been dedicated to the goddess Isis, one of the most important goddesses in ancient Egyptian religion. The discovery includes the remains of the temple's foundations, columns, and walls, as well as statues, pottery, and inscriptions. Archaeologists say the temple was probably built during the reign of the Roman Emperor Hadrian in the 2nd century AD, and it's one of the few Roman-era temples ever found in Alexandria. The discovery is providing new insights into the religious and cultural life of Alexandria during the Roman period, when the city was one of the most important and prosperous cities in the Mediterranean world.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Male + American Female)
paras: Man (Mark): Hey Lisa, I heard you joined a gym recently. How's that going?
Woman (Lisa): It's going pretty well! I've been going about three times a week for the past month. I'm still getting used to it, but I already feel better.
Man: That's great! What made you decide to join a gym?

Woman: Well, I've been feeling really out of shape lately. I sit at a desk all day for work, and I don't get much exercise. I've also been having trouble sleeping and I've been feeling stressed all the time. My doctor said I should start exercising regularly, so I finally decided to do it.
Man: Yeah, exercise is great for both physical and mental health. What kind of stuff do you do at the gym?

Woman: Mostly I've been using the cardio machines—treadmill, elliptical, stationary bike. I try to do about 30 minutes of cardio each time. But I'm not really sure what else to do. I see all these weight machines and I don't know how to use them, and I'm kind of embarrassed to ask.
Man: Oh, I know what you mean. It can be intimidating at first. Have you tried any group classes?
Woman: No, I haven't. I've thought about it, but I'm kind of nervous. I don't want to be the worst one in the class.

Man: Ha, everyone feels that way at first! Group classes are actually great because you have an instructor to show you what to do, and it's more fun than working out alone. There are all kinds of classes—yoga, spinning, Zumba, kickboxing... you should try one.
Woman: Maybe I will. Which ones do you like?

Man: I really like the strength training classes. They're a good way to learn proper form for lifting weights, and you get a full-body workout. I also like yoga for stretching and relaxation. It's great for stress relief.
Woman: That sounds good. I should try a yoga class. I've heard it's good for flexibility and stress.
Man: Definitely. And most gyms let you try a class for free the first time, right? You could go to a beginner class and see how you like it.
Woman: Yeah, I think they do. What about weights? Should I be lifting weights too?

Man: Absolutely! Strength training is really important, especially as you get older. It helps build muscle, which boosts your metabolism and keeps your bones strong. And you don't have to lift heavy weights to get benefits—even light weights or bodyweight exercises can make a big difference.
Woman: I didn't know that. I always thought lifting weights was just for people who want to get really big muscles.

Man: No, that's a common misconception. Everyone can benefit from strength training. If you want, I could show you some basic exercises next time we're both at the gym. I'm not an expert or anything, but I know the basics.
Woman: Really? That would be great! I'd really appreciate that.
Man: No problem! How about this Thursday evening? We can meet at the gym around 6 and I'll show you around the weight area and teach you a few exercises.
Woman: Perfect! Thanks so much, Mark. I've been wanting to try weights but I was too scared to just jump in.
Man: No worries! Everyone starts somewhere. And hey, if you end up liking it, we could even work out together sometimes. It's more fun with a partner.
Woman: That sounds great. I'd like that.

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Sophie): Hey James, I need your advice. I'm planning a trip to Japan next spring, and I'm so excited! But I'm also a little overwhelmed with all the planning.
Man (James): Japan? That's awesome! I've been twice, so I might be able to help. What do you need advice on?
Woman: Well, first of all, I'm a vegetarian, and I'm worried about finding food I can eat. Is it hard to be vegetarian in Japan?

Man: Hmm, that's a good question. It's definitely easier in big cities like Tokyo and Kyoto, but it can be tricky in smaller towns. A lot of Japanese food uses fish broth or bonito flakes, even in dishes that seem vegetarian. But don't worry—there are still plenty of options. Tofu is everywhere, and there are lots of vegetable dishes. You just have to be careful and ask about the ingredients.
Woman: That's good to know. What about transportation? What's the best way to get around?

Man: The bullet train, or Shinkansen, is amazing—it's fast, comfortable, and super reliable. It's a bit expensive, but if you're traveling between cities, it's definitely worth it. You should get a Japan Rail Pass if you're going to be traveling a lot—it saves you a lot of money. Within cities, the subway systems are excellent and really easy to use, even if you don't speak Japanese.
Woman: Great. What about etiquette? Are there things I should know about Japanese customs so I don't accidentally offend anyone?

Man: Oh, there are a few important ones. First, you take off your shoes when you enter someone's home, and also in many traditional restaurants, temples, and shrines. Second, it's considered rude to talk on your phone on trains—you should keep your phone on silent and text instead. Third, tipping is not a thing in Japan—in fact, it can be considered rude. Just pay the bill as is.
Woman: Oh, interesting. I didn't know about the tipping thing. What else?

Man: Oh, and when you're eating noodles like ramen, it's actually polite to slurp them loudly. It shows you're enjoying the food. I know that sounds weird if you're not used to it, but it's totally normal in Japan.
Woman: Ha, that's funny. I'll have to practice my slurping. What about the cherry blossoms? I'm going in spring, so I want to see them. When's the best time?

Man: That depends on where you're going. Cherry blossom season moves from south to north as the weather warms up. In Kyoto and Tokyo, it's usually around late March to early April. But it's hard to predict exactly—it depends on the weather. You should check the cherry blossom forecast closer to your trip.
Woman: Yeah, I've heard it's really unpredictable. What are some must-see places?

Man: Well, Tokyo is a must—there's so much to see and do there. Kyoto is also amazing—lots of temples, shrines, and traditional culture. If you have time, I'd also recommend going to Hiroshima to see the Peace Memorial Park, and maybe a day trip to Miyajima Island to see the famous floating torii gate.
Woman: That all sounds incredible. I'm getting even more excited now. Thanks so much for all the advice, James. You've been really helpful.
Man: No problem! I'm jealous—Japan is one of my favorite places. You're going to have an amazing time. And if you have any more questions as you plan, just ask.
Woman: I will! Thanks again.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Female)
paras: The history of chocolate is a fascinating story that spans over 3,000 years and multiple continents. From its origins as a bitter drink in ancient Mesoamerica to the sweet, creamy treat we know today, chocolate has come a long way.

The history of chocolate begins in Central America, where the Olmec, Maya, and Aztec civilizations grew cacao trees and made a bitter drink from cacao beans. The Maya and Aztecs believed cacao was a gift from the gods, and it was used in religious ceremonies, as currency, and as a luxury drink for the wealthy. The drink was made by roasting and grinding cacao beans into a paste, then mixing it with water, chili peppers, and other spices. It was nothing like the sweet chocolate we know today.

Chocolate was brought to Europe by Spanish explorers in the 16th century. The Spanish added sugar and cinnamon to the bitter cacao drink, making it sweeter and more palatable. At first, chocolate was a luxury that only the wealthy and noble could afford. It was served in royal courts and elite social gatherings, and it became a symbol of wealth and status.

As chocolate became more popular, European powers established cacao plantations in their colonies in the Americas, using enslaved labor to grow and process cacao. The demand for chocolate continued to grow, and by the 18th century, chocolate houses were popular meeting places in cities like London and Paris.

The Industrial Revolution in the 19th century transformed chocolate from an expensive luxury drink into an affordable, mass-produced food. New inventions like the cocoa press, which separated cocoa butter from cocoa powder, made it possible to produce solid chocolate bars. Companies like Cadbury, Nestlé, and Lindt pioneered new chocolate-making techniques and began producing the milk chocolate bars and candies we're familiar with today.

In the 20th century, chocolate became even more accessible and affordable, and it became one of the most popular foods in the world. Today, people all over the world eat billions of dollars worth of chocolate every year, in everything from candy bars and cookies to ice cream and hot cocoa.

In recent years, there has been growing interest in dark chocolate, which has higher cocoa content and is often considered healthier than milk chocolate. Studies have shown that dark chocolate, when eaten in moderation, may have health benefits due to its antioxidant content.

But the chocolate industry also faces challenges, including issues with child labor and poverty in cacao-growing regions. Many farmers earn very little money, and there are ongoing efforts to make the chocolate industry more fair and sustainable.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Male)
paras: Dreams have fascinated humans for thousands of years. From ancient civilizations who believed dreams were messages from the gods to modern scientists studying the brain, we've always wondered why we dream and what our dreams mean. While we still don't have all the answers, research has taught us a lot about dreaming.

Most dreaming happens during REM (rapid eye movement) sleep, a stage of sleep where the brain is very active and the eyes move rapidly back and forth under the eyelids. We usually have several REM periods throughout the night, and we can have multiple dreams each night, though we don't remember most of them. In fact, most people forget 90 to 95 percent of their dreams within minutes of waking up.

There are many theories about why we dream. One of the most famous theories comes from Sigmund Freud, who believed that dreams are a window into the unconscious mind, revealing our hidden desires, fears, and conflicts. While Freud's ideas are still influential, many modern scientists don't agree with his specific interpretations.

Another theory is the activation-synthesis theory, which suggests that dreams are just the brain's way of making sense of random neural activity during REM sleep. According to this theory, the brain tries to create a story or narrative out of the random signals it's receiving, and that's what we experience as a dream.

Other theories suggest that dreams help us process emotions, consolidate memories, solve problems, or practice dealing with threatening situations. There's evidence to support all of these ideas, and it's likely that dreaming serves multiple functions rather than just one.

One interesting phenomenon is lucid dreaming—when you become aware that you're dreaming while you're still in the dream. Some people can even learn to control their dreams, changing the plot, characters, and environment. Lucid dreaming has become a popular topic of research, and some people practice techniques to increase their chances of having lucid dreams.

Dreams can also have a big impact on our waking lives. A bad dream or nightmare can affect our mood for hours after we wake up. And sometimes people have creative insights or solve problems in their dreams—many famous inventions, scientific discoveries, and works of art have been inspired by dreams.

While we've learned a lot about dreaming, there's still much we don't understand. Dreams remain one of the great mysteries of the human mind, and they continue to fascinate scientists and ordinary people alike.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: Public libraries are one of the most important institutions in modern society, yet many people take them for granted. In an age of digital information and e-books, some people have even predicted that libraries would become obsolete. But in reality, public libraries are more important than ever, and they continue to evolve to meet the changing needs of their communities.

At their core, public libraries are about providing free and equal access to information and knowledge for everyone, regardless of income, background, or status. This is a radical idea when you think about it—in a world where so much is behind paywalls and only available to those who can afford it, libraries offer books, computers, internet access, and many other resources for free.

But modern libraries are much more than just buildings full of books. They're community centers that offer a wide range of services and programs. Many libraries offer free classes and workshops on everything from computer skills to job searching to creative writing. They host story times for children, book clubs for adults, and lectures and events for the whole community.

Libraries also play a crucial role in bridging the digital divide. Not everyone has access to a computer or high-speed internet at home, and libraries provide free access to both. This is especially important for low-income families, students, job seekers, and older adults. In many communities, libraries are the only place where people can go online for free.

Another important function of libraries is providing access to information and supporting literacy. They help children develop reading skills and a love of books. They help adults improve their literacy and learn new skills. And they provide access to reliable information in an era of misinformation and fake news. Librarians are trained to help people find accurate, trustworthy information, which is an incredibly valuable service.

Libraries also serve as safe, welcoming public spaces. They're one of the few remaining places where you can go and stay for as long as you want without having to buy anything. They're warm in the winter, cool in the summer, and they're open to everyone. For many people—especially those who are homeless, unemployed, or just lonely—libraries are a lifeline.

Despite all these benefits, many public libraries face challenges. Budget cuts are common, and libraries often have to do more with less. But communities that invest in their libraries see real benefits—better education outcomes, stronger communities, and more opportunities for everyone.

In a world that's increasingly digital and divided, public libraries remind us that knowledge and information should be accessible to everyone, not just those who can afford it. They're one of the cornerstones of a democratic and equitable society.
